name: QTS Irving - Dallas Data Center Campus

profile.campus: Irving, Dallas County, Texas (QTS Irving 1 campus, one of QTS's two Dallas-area mega-scale campuses)
profile.reading:
Per QTS's own facility page, the Irving 1 campus comprises six buildings across several Longhorn Drive addresses (DC1 and DC2 at 6431 Longhorn Dr, DC3 at 6351, DC4 at 6311, DC5 at 6300, DC6 at 6440), totaling a 56-acre campus with 165+ MW of critical campus capacity, LEED Gold certification, renewable energy sourcing availability, a redundant campus fiber conduit system connecting each building, and on-site EV charging. QTS describes Irving as one of its two mega-scale Dallas-area campuses alongside Fort Worth, tracked elsewhere in this registry.

QTS was founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas, and was taken private in a roughly $10 billion Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT)-led acquisition completed August 31, 2021, per Blackstone's own press release; QTS is no longer an independent SEC filer.

QTS positions itself as a "hyperscale-neutral" wholesale and colocation landlord, leasing built data center capacity to enterprise, cloud, and hyperscale tenants rather than operating its own end-user cloud service, a business model it shares with peers such as Digital Realty and CyrusOne. Since Blackstone completed its roughly $10 billion take-private acquisition in August 2021, QTS has continued expanding across multiple US metros rather than slowing development, including major campus filings and expansions in Phoenix (a 750MW, 375-acre Glendale campus acquired for $255.3 million in July 2022) and Dallas-Fort Worth (its two mega-scale Irving and Fort Worth campuses), consistent with the scale of buildout QTS has also pursued in Northern Virginia, Georgia, and Ohio, tracked elsewhere in this registry.

QTS was originally founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas by Chad Williams, and grew through a mix of acquisitions and ground-up construction into a national wholesale/colocation platform before its 2013 IPO as a publicly traded REIT; that public period ended with the 2021 Blackstone take-private deal. QTS's current published portfolio language describes over 30 facilities across North America and Europe on its own site, while Wikipedia gives a somewhat different approximate figure of 28 locations across 16 US states plus two Netherlands sites (Eemshaven and Groningen), a discrepancy this registry notes rather than resolves in favor of either source.

reading.body:
QTS Irving 1 is a six-building, 56-acre campus in Dallas County rated at 165 MW of critical capacity across two primary facility codes. The operator publishes only a campus total, not per-building breakdown or IT load allocation. Assuming 40 kW per rack as a common AI training density, 165 MW implies roughly 4,100 racks if fully utilized for compute, though the published figure conflates all critical load and does not specify the split between power, cooling, and IT. The campus holds LEED Gold certification and includes on-site EV charging and a fiber conduit system connecting all six buildings.

Irving 1 ranks 19th among the 18 Texas facilities this registry has found with published MW figures, placing it outside the top tier of published capacity in the state. Of 468 MW published across Texas data center campuses, Irving 1 accounts for approximately 35 percent if the 165 MW figure is accurate. Texas has 133 mapped facilities total, of which only 18 have published specs, indicating that most capacity in the state remains undisclosed.

QTS operates the campus as a wholesale landlord under Blackstone ownership since August 2021 and positions itself as hyperscale-neutral rather than as an operator of its own cloud services. Whether this campus matters to AI depends on the portion of its 165 MW available and configured for accelerator workloads, a detail QTS does not publish. The lack of per-building or IT-specific power allocation prevents ranking Irving 1 against competing campuses on compute density or available rack count.
